title: Small multiples of prediction against reference: one panel per variable, plus the curves and drifts that back them up
summary: These SciML figures check a surrogate of an ignition problem the way an engineer would: a training and validation curve pair, a grid with one panel per species and temperature at a fixed condition, a replication grid at four conditions, and the drift of conserved elements.

media.alt: A grid of small line plots with one panel per variable: several species mass fractions and temperature against time. Each panel has a solid green reference curve and a dashed red prediction that follows it closely for most species and departs for trace species. Two inert species are flat. The panel titles name the variable; the legend appears only in the first panel.

read_the_figure.question: For which variables, and at which times, does the prediction depart from the reference, and is anything that should be conserved drifting?
read_the_figure.axes: Species grid: time in milliseconds from 0 to 2 on every panel, mass fraction on the vertical axis (different scale per panel), 11 panels (eight reacting species, two inert, temperature). Replication grid: four rows of conditions (initial temperature and equivalence ratio in the left axis label) by five columns of variables, time in ms. Training curves: epoch to 12 000, loss on a log axis, fit loss and a derivative-matching loss; a second panel with the validation loss. Drift figure: time against the absolute drift of an element's mass fraction on a log axis.
look_at: Compare dashed red to solid green panel by panel before looking at any aggregate number. Major species lie on top of each other; intermediates peak early and are the first to deviate; trace radicals show the largest relative gaps.
Inert species (argon, nitrogen) should be flat lines that coincide. If they are not, the pipeline, not the physics, is wrong.
A panel title that carries a percentage (a temperature or enthalpy change) can be above 100 percent: that is a signal to check the normalization it uses before trusting it.

Replication grid: the legend names the reference solver and two model variants. On this still the dashed model curves are drawn as flat lines at the initial state while the reference rises sharply; whether that is a plotting problem or the model, the figure alone cannot say. That is exactly why a printed error per panel matters.

Training curves: the fit loss falls steadily with spikes; the validation loss falls then flattens at about the same epoch where it stops improving and creeps up slowly. The curve on the right is the one that matters.
Drift: both models drift upward over the 0.6 ms shown, at the 1e-4 level for the element mass fractions; which model is lower differs between the two elements.
read_the_figure.proves: Small multiples show where the model fails and by how much on each variable, which a single aggregate error hides. A drift plot tests a physical law the loss never asked for.
if_wrong: Dashed curve that cannot be seen: draw it thicker or add the error beneath; a missing model curve looks like perfect agreement or total failure.
A validation loss that rises while training loss falls: overfitting; stop earlier.
Element drift that grows monotonically: the model does not conserve mass; the error accumulates over longer rollouts.
Different vertical scales per panel: fine for shape, but compare errors on a common relative scale.
must_check: That each panel states its variable and unit and that the reference is the one drawn solid.
That an error number is printed per panel or in a table.
That training and validation curves use the same loss.
That drift is plotted for each conserved quantity on a log axis, with the tolerance.

terms.meaning: A cheap model that stands in for an expensive simulation.
The trusted result, here from a standard chemical kinetics solver, against which the model is judged.
A loss that fits both the values and their time derivatives.
The mass fraction of an element summed over all species; conserved in a closed reacting system.
Stopping at the epoch of lowest validation loss.
Species that do not react, so their mass fractions are constant.

remember: Look at the picture before the number; then check the number.
Element masses are conserved in a closed reactor; a model that does not conserve them is not a faithful surrogate.
Validation loss, not training loss, tells you when to stop.
Inert species are free sanity checks.
A model curve that is invisible, flat or clipped should never pass without a numerical error.

steps.title: Element mass fraction
steps.note: n is the number of atoms of element e in species k, W the molar masses. The drift plot shows the absolute difference between Z_e(t) and Z_e(0) for the model.

steps.title: Drift as a diagnostic
steps.note: For an exact solver it stays at round-off. For a learned model it grows with the rollout length, so a figure should state the horizon.

steps.title: A derivative-matching loss
steps.note: Matching slopes as well as values penalizes a flat prediction that has the right average; the two curves in the training figure are two versions of this fit.

steps.title: When validation stops improving
steps.note: The epoch of the minimum of the right-hand curve. Epochs beyond it only fit the training conditions better.

worked.title: Hydrogen element fraction carried by water
worked.problem: Water has mass fraction 0.17 (read off a panel). Hydrogen is 2 atoms of molar mass 1.008 in water of molar mass 18.015. How much hydrogen element mass fraction does water carry?

solution.text: The hydrogen share of water by mass.

worked.answer: About 0.019; the sum over all hydrogen-bearing species stays constant in the reference, so the model's sum can be compared with it.

analyze.q: In the species grid, which variables would you expect to deviate first and why do they dominate relative error?
The validation curve flattens while training loss keeps falling. What decision follows, and what number would you report?
The dashed model curves in the replication grid look flat. List two checks that would tell a plotting error from a model failure.
analyze.hint: Print values; plot the same data numerically.

evaluate.q: Rank the importance of: per-panel error, drift, training curve. Which one would you refuse to publish without?
evaluate.hint: Think of what each rules out.

evaluate.q: A drift of 1e-4 over 0.6 ms: acceptable? What else do you need to decide?

create: Add a row under each panel of the species grid showing the relative error on a log axis and a dotted tolerance line.
Design a figure that overlays model drift for several rollout horizons and fits a growth law to it.

checks.q: What should the two inert species look like?
An element mass fraction starts at 0.0250 and ends a rollout at 0.0252. Drift?
Why do trace species show the largest gaps in a relative sense?
checks.answer: Their true values are tiny, so small absolute errors are large fractions.

checks.q: A validation loss that rises slowly after epoch 8000: is it a problem?
checks.answer: It signals fitting the training conditions at the expense of held-out ones; report the checkpoint at the minimum.

checks.q: Suggest a layout that keeps the benefits of the grid but makes errors comparable.
checks.answer: A second row of panels with relative error on a shared log axis, or one summary panel of error per variable.
